one_liner: Header-only C++11 serialization library whose binary archive round-tripped a 17 KB record ~2.2x faster than Protobuf in 2019.
what_it_does: cereal converts C++ objects to and from binary, portable-binary, JSON or XML archives using a serialize() template (or save/load pair) you write per type as a member or free function, and standard-library types such as containers, smart pointers, optional, variant and chrono work once you include the matching cereal/types/*.hpp header. Archives wrap a std::ostream or std::istream and are called like functions, ar(x, y, z). There is no IDL or code generator, so it cannot drop in for Protobuf: your C++ struct is the schema, and only cereal code with matching serialize functions can read the data.
how_it_is_fast: Dispatch happens at compile time: SFINAE traits pick each type's member or free serialize/save/load, and variadic ar(...) calls inline down to the archive's primitive writers. The binary archive writes each arithmetic value's native bytes with one streambuf sputn/sgetn call, and a contiguous arithmetic vector or string is a uint64 length tag plus one bulk binary_data copy, with no field tags, no varint/zigzag coding and no per-element framing (the benchmark payload is exactly 8 + 1000x8 + 8 + 100x(8+86) = 17,416 bytes). Only shared_ptr targets are tracked (an address-to-id hash map), and version numbers are written only for types that opt in, so plain structs carry no metadata. Protobuf varint-encodes each int64 and tags each string, which makes its payload smaller (16,116 bytes) but its round trip slower here.
when_to_use: C++-to-C++ data where both ends are built from the same code: checkpoints, caches, save state, or IPC between builds of one codebase
Records dominated by contiguous arithmetic vectors and strings, which take the single-memcpy path. The benchmark record was 1,000 int64 plus 100 strings of 86 chars.
Serializing existing STL-heavy types (maps, shared_ptr/unique_ptr, optional, variant) without writing a .proto file or adding a codegen step
Migrating off Boost.Serialization: the syntax is similar (CEREAL_CLASS_VERSION mirrors BOOST_CLASS_VERSION), there is no Boost dependency, and it ran slightly faster in the same shootout
When one serialize() function should also produce human-readable JSON or XML for debugging
when_not_to_use: Cross-language interchange or schema evolution. The binary format is positional and untagged, so reordering or changing fields breaks old data unless you opt into versioning. The docs say cereal was not designed as a robust long-term storage format.

Untrusted input (network peers, user files). Container sizes read from the stream go straight into resize(). The maintainer closed #103 saying cereal expects to produce its own data and will not add checks. #629 reports a null-pointer dereference loading untrusted XML (still open), and #870 reported a type-confusion bug in 1.3.2 and earlier (closed, details redacted).
Size-sensitive wire formats. Integers and length tags are fixed-width (uint64 size tags), so the benchmark payload was 17,416 bytes vs 16,116 for Protobuf and 13,402 for msgpack.

Chasing the fastest possible round trip. In the same table yas (302.7 ms) was ~3.5x faster than cereal. Cap'n Proto and FlatBuffers finished a build+serialize+deserialize cycle in 400.98 and 491.5 ms.
Raw-pointer or reference object graphs, and shared_ptr aliasing constructors. None of these are supported; Boost.Serialization handles raw pointers.

integration.dependencies: none. The JSON and XML archives use bundled RapidJSON, RapidXML and base64 headers. Building the repo's own tests/sandbox needs Boost.Serialization unless SKIP_PERFORMANCE_COMPARISON or JUST_INSTALL_CEREAL is set.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11. The docs name g++ 4.7.3, clang++ 3.3 and MSVC 2013 or newer. CI covers g++ 4.7 and up, Xcode 15/16 clang and VS2013-2022. std::optional/std::variant support needs C++17. The CMake minimum is 3.6.
integration.platforms: any with a conforming C++11 compiler (Linux, macOS, Windows in CI). BinaryArchive is native-endian, so use PortableBinaryArchive when data crosses endianness.
integration.thread_safety: Never use one archive from several threads at once. Separate archives can run in parallel only if CEREAL_THREAD_SAFE=1 is defined before every cereal include (or via the CMake THREAD_SAFE option). That setting mutex-guards the global polymorphism and versioning registries; the default is no locking.

gotchas: Versioning is opt-in and all-or-nothing per type. Loading data saved without a version through a versioned serialize function corrupts the load and will likely crash. Load with the same cereal version you saved with.
Archives are only guaranteed to have flushed when destroyed, and XML/JSON write nothing until then, so scope archives with RAII. Open file streams with std::ios::binary for binary archives.

Polymorphic pointers need CEREAL_REGISTER_TYPE and RTTI, and registration only binds to archives #included before it. Registering inside a Windows DLL needs CEREAL_REGISTER_DYNAMIC_INIT/CEREAL_FORCE_DYNAMIC_INIT. Errors throw cereal::Exception (a std::runtime_error), so exceptions must be enabled.

Known bugs: CVE-2020-11105 (shared_ptr ids keyed by raw address) is fixed only in 1.3.1+. CVE-2020-11104 (#625, open): long double writes uninitialized padding bytes. #880 (open, 2026): the bundled RapidJSON misparses some doubles under MSVC /O1 /GL /LTCG.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick cereal over Boost.Serialization when you want the same member serialize() style without Boost and can do without raw pointers; it was ~1.14x faster in the same table (1052.46 vs 1195.04 ms). Pick hpp-proto if you must keep Protobuf schemas or wire data, and Apache Thrift's binary protocol (1190.22 ms in the same table) if you need a schema shared with non-C++ code.
verified_claims_summary: In thekvs/cpp-serializers (2019; cereal 1.2.2, protobuf 3.7.0, msgpack 3.1.1; CMake Release build, with clang 5.0.0 named by the README revision that published the table; an unspecified 'Intel Core i7' on Ubuntu 16.04), round-tripping one record of 1,000 int64 and 100 strings of 86 chars through cereal's BinaryOutputArchive/BinaryInputArchive took 1052.46 ms in total vs 2312.78 ms for Protobuf (~2.2x) and 2560.6 ms for msgpack (~2.4x), with no std:: baseline involved. Each cereal iteration builds a fresh std::ostringstream and std::stringstream and copies the buffer while the Protobuf loop reuses its message and string, so the stream overhead is inside cereal's number.
status_note: Lightly maintained (last release v1.3.2 in Feb 2022, master commits since 2024 are compiler and CI fixes with the latest on 2026-03-11, and an open issue asks for a new release), but it is BSD-3-Clause and header-only, so vendoring 1.3.2 or master is easy.
